Ambition

/am-BISH-un/ · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Ambition means a strong desire to achieve something, requiring determination.

Ambition means a strong desire to achieve something, requiring determination. Her ambition to map the deepest cave systems shaped every choice she made after graduation.

Worked Example

At fourteen, Tobias announced that he would one day design a bridge people would cross for a century. His notebooks filled with sketches of arches and cable stays. He chose his university, his internships, and even his city by how much closer each brought him to major structural projects. Colleagues twice his age noticed that he never drifted: every year was another deliberate step. That single, driving ambition organized his entire career.

Tobias's strong desire for one great achievement — a desire that steers his choices for decades — is what ambition means.

How Ambition Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

drive

drive: inner energy pushing toward goals

determination

determination: firmness of purpose

Antonyms

apathy

apathy: lack of interest or desire

complacency

complacency: smug satisfaction with things as they are

How Strong Is It? — motivation → ambition → obsession

motivation vs. ambition

motivation vs. ambition: Motivation is the weaker, everyday fuel — enough to start today's task; ambition is a strong desire aimed at big achievements across years.

obsession vs. ambition

obsession vs. ambition: Obsession is stronger than ambition, and darker: an obsession crowds out everything else in life, while ambition can still share the room.

Sort It Out

Now place each word on the right side of ambition.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — amb-

Prefix — amb-: around (Latin ambi-)

Root — it

Root — it: to go (Latin ire)

Suffix — -ion

Suffix — -ion: noun-forming: act or state of

Put it together

Put it together: Ambition comes from Latin ambitio, 'a going around': ambi- (around) plus ire (to go). In Rome it described candidates literally walking around the forum canvassing for votes — a hungry circuit in pursuit of office. The going root ire still moves through English in exit ('he goes out'), transit (a going across), and itinerary (the plan of where you will go).

Use the root in a new word: exit

Use the root in a new word: exit: The crowd streamed toward the exit — exit is literally 'he goes out' in Latin, from the same verb ire (to go) that pictures ambition as going around in pursuit of a goal.

Root Check

Word Choice

neutral; can shade admiring or critical

Ambition is the noun and aspire (also in this unit) is its verb-of-motion: to aspire to a goal is to hold an ambition for it. English is two-minded about the word — 'healthy ambition' praises drive, while 'blind ambition' warns of wanting success at any cost.
